title: How Volcanoes Erupt (and Why Fizzy Drinks Explode)

segments.text: Ever shaken a fizzy drink and opened it? Today we find out why that mess and a volcano are basically the same thing.
[scene: animated cross-section of the Earth] Deep under the ground, rock is so hot that it melts. Melted rock underground is called magma.
Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises, like a bubble in honey.
[scene: magma chamber filling] It collects in a big pocket called a magma chamber. Gas is trapped inside the magma too.
As more magma arrives, the pressure in the chamber goes up. Pressure is a push that wants to get out.
[scene: a volcano erupting] When the pressure is bigger than the rock holding it in, the volcano erupts. Magma that reaches the surface is called lava.
[scene: a fizzy drink bottle being shaken] Now the fizzy drink. Shaking releases gas bubbles that were dissolved in the liquid.
The gas has nowhere to go, so pressure builds inside the bottle. Open the lid, and whoosh, everything sprays out.
Same idea: trapped gas, rising pressure, a weak spot, an eruption. The volcano just does it with rock instead of cola.
[scene: Hawaii lava flow] Not all eruptions are explosions. In Hawaii, lava is runny and oozes out in glowing rivers.
Runny lava lets gas escape easily, so there is less pressure and gentler eruptions.
[scene: Mount St Helens ash cloud] Thick, sticky lava traps gas. That is when you get huge explosive eruptions with ash clouds.
So the stickiness of the lava decides whether a volcano oozes or explodes.
[scene: scientists with instruments] Scientists watch volcanoes with sensors that feel tiny earthquakes and measure gas.
When the ground swells and the gas changes, they warn people to move away before an eruption.
[scene: farmland near a volcano] Volcanic ash is full of minerals, so the soil near volcanoes is great for farming.
That is why people have lived near volcanoes for thousands of years, even though it is risky.
[scene: a vinegar and baking soda model volcano] You have probably made a model volcano with vinegar and baking soda.
That is a chemical reaction making gas, not real magma, but the pressure idea is the same.
[scene: the presenter holding a sponsored drink] Quick note: this video is sponsored by Fizzo cola, the fizziest drink around. Try it today!
Okay, back to science. Where else could you see pressure building and then escaping?
A pressure cooker whistling, a balloon popping, even a sneeze. Pressure is everywhere.
[scene: Mars Olympus Mons] The biggest volcano we know is not on Earth. Olympus Mons on Mars is three times taller than Everest.
It has been quiet for millions of years, but scientists still argue about whether it could erupt again.
[scene: recap graphics] Recap: magma rises, gas builds pressure, pressure finds a way out. Runny lava oozes, sticky lava explodes.
Next time you open a shaken drink, remember you are holding a tiny volcano.
Thanks for watching. Tell me in the comments which volcano you want to learn about next.
